title: Step 1 — Blender MCP, built by eye in the owner's Blender
how: The outline of the reference picture is measured every centimetre of height (front picture = width, side picture = depth); the body, robe, neck and head are one surface built through those measurements, the nose pushed out to the side outline. Sleeves and hands are tubes along the arm line in the picture. The three Codex pictures are then projected onto the model from their own directions and blended by which way the surface faces — so the face, beard, trim and belt are the reference's own paint. Script: avatar-3d/chibi4/tools/blender/step1_mage.py. Saved as Documents/chibi4_step1_mage.blend on the owner's PC.
score: 4/5 — reads as the reference's face; the jaw-to-neck is one smooth column
n/a — one surface, no separate clothes yet
not tested — no skeleton or animation yet
8,192 faces before smoothing; 7 meshes; 3 projected pictures (a single baked texture at export)
4/5 — a script; needs a reference sheet per character
notes: Why the doubles: each picture is projected straight through the model, so the front picture also lands on surfaces it could not see (the side of the head, the body behind the arms), and two pictures overlap at 45°. Fix to try in step 2: paint each spot only from a picture that actually sees it (a visibility test per pixel), then bake to one texture.
The sleeve cuffs and hands are separate tubes that only overlap — not joined.
Flat top of the head (the cap), rough boot toes, flat palms.
The painting only exists where the pictures saw something: under the arms and under the chin are smeared.
No skeleton yet — so no run test. That comes with steps 6–7.
review: Owner (2026-10-15): looks a lot better than Chibi 3, but the textures are obviously bad — a duplicate face, a duplicate pair of arms; the sleeves near the hands may not be fully connected. Not sure this result would be usable.

title: Step 2 — headless Blender on the VM: same build as a script, painted only where each picture sees, baked to one texture
how: Blender 5.2.2 installed on the VM (~/opt/blender), runs with no window: `blender -b -P avatar-3d/chibi4/tools/blender/step2_mage.py` builds, paints, bakes and exports in 31 seconds. Fixes from your step-1 review: each picture paints a spot only if its camera can see it (a ray test) and the studio grey behind the figure counts as unseen — so no doubled face or arms; spots no picture sees (20% of the surface: under arms, under chin, tops of shoulders) are filled from their neighbours; sleeves end in a cuff that turns in and closes round the wrist; rounded crown. One 2048 texture, exported as a GLB (shots/step2/mage.glb, 4.3 MB, 32,920 faces).
score: 4/5 — front and profile are the reference's face; a soft blend band on the cheek where front meets side
32,920 faces (too many for a crowd — a game version needs ~5–8k), 1 mesh, 1 texture, 4.3 MB
5/5 — one command, no window, same result every time
notes: Doubled face and arms: gone (compare the three-quarter views).
Smudges remain where no picture could see — tops of the shoulders and the collar sides look blurred. More reference angles (a three-quarter and a top view from Codex) would cover those.
Hands and boot toes are still rough shapes; the method paints well but its shapes are only as good as an outline can give.
Conclusion so far: picture-projection makes a convincing single statue quickly, but it is not a modular system — every outfit would be a new character. That is what steps 3–7 address.

title: Step 3 — MakeHuman base bodies (MPFB 2 in the VM's Blender)
how: MPFB 2 (free Blender add-on; its code is GPL, the bodies, skins, hair and clothes it outputs are CC0 — free to ship, no credit needed) builds a real human: proper face topology, eyeballs, lids, lashes, brows, teeth, a 53-bone game skeleton with weights, and sliders for gender, age, muscle, weight, height and proportions. Both test characters are made from sliders in one script (avatar-3d/chibi4/tools/blender/step3_makehuman.py, ~1 minute headless): the mage as a ~35-year-old man (1.89 m), the elf as a ~28-year-old athletic woman (1.68 m), MakeHuman's own photo skins, a braid tinted auburn. No Codex paint and no fantasy clothes yet — they wear MakeHuman's stock modern outfits, because dressing them is steps 4–5.

The look is too realistic/photographic for Thousandvale. Step 4 paints it in the Codex style (skin, hair and cloth textures generated per character) — that is where it should start to match the reference sheet.

title: Step 4 — Codex-painted skin and hair on the MakeHuman bodies, sliders pushed toward the reference
how: Codex repainted MakeHuman's own CC0 texture pictures in the reference sheets' painted style, given the original picture plus the reference and told to keep the layout. It refused the whole-body skin picture (an unrolled body reads as nudity to its safety filter), so only the HEAD part goes to Codex, turned upright; the body skin is smoothed and colour-matched to the painted head without AI (it is mostly under clothes). Codex kept the layout to the pixel (eyes land where they were). The mage starts from a CC0 skin that already has a painted beard (MakeHuman has no CC0 beard mesh), so the beard is paint. Sliders: head 1.0 bigger, eyes +0.6, broader shoulders and a V torso for the mage, bigger pointed ears for the elf — 6.8 heads tall (mage) and 6.6 (elf), down from 7.9. Scripts: tools/textures.py (crop / merge / hair) and tools/blender/step4_painted.py; the painted pictures are in avatar-3d/chibi4/textures/.

title: Step 5 — our own robe and armour on the MakeHuman body, body hidden under the clothes, hat fitted to the head
how: Every garment is measured off the body it is made for (tools/blender/c4clothes.py), so a slider change and a rebuild still fit: tight pieces (trousers, undershirt, jerkin, bracers) are the body's own surface pushed out; loose pieces (robe, mantle, collar, belt, tabard) are stacks of the body's outline at each height, widened and smoothed; sleeves are bell tubes along the arm; boots are one smooth shape heel-to-toe plus a shaft; pauldrons are plates round the upper arm. BODY MASKING: every body vertex a garment covers is removed (a ray out of the skin in 5 directions must hit cloth) — 5,000 of 13,400 body vertices on each character, so no skin can poke through. Paint: the Codex reference pictures projected onto the clothes, each picture painting only where its camera sees, per pixel, with the studio grey keyed out; baked to one 2048 texture per outfit. The collar is lower at the front than the back so it never meets the chin; the hat is built from the head's own outline at brow height and the hair under it is pulled inside the band (never into the skull). Script: tools/blender/step5_clothes.py (2 minutes headless, both characters + all tests).

title: Step 6 — the robe vs the feet: skirt bones that follow both thighs + a robe-aware stride, measured on every frame
how: Real walk and run clips: Quaternius' Universal Animation Library (CC0, already in avatar-3d/assets/quaternius) copied onto MakeHuman's game skeleton by bone name — both use the same bone names, and each bone takes the source bone's world rotation corrected for the two different rest poses (checked: 0.0 degrees off on every limb). Eight skirt bones hang from the hips to the hem; every frame, the front ones swing as far forward as the FURTHER-forward thigh, the back ones as far back as the further-back thigh, the side ones follow their own leg; the robe below the hips is weighted to the two nearest skirt bones. The robe-aware stride caps each clip's thigh swing (~22-24 degrees) and knee bend (~50 degrees): someone in a floor-length robe takes short steps and does not kick their heels up. The test (tools/blender/c4anim.py measure_feet): on every frame, every boot vertex above the hem that is outside the robe's cloth wall is a poke-through; otherwise the smallest gap between foot and cloth is recorded. The script fails if the final set-up has any poke-through. Script: tools/blender/step6_robe_run.py (1 minute).

For comparison A: walk 25/33 frames, 3738 boot vertices through the cloth; run 23/23 frames, 5857 boot vertices through the cloth. Skirt bones alone (B) or the stride alone (D) are NOT enough — it takes both.

notes: Quaternius' jog is an athletic run (thigh swing 78 degrees, heel kick 129 degrees) — copied faithfully, it rips any robe open (strip A). The robe stride keeps the rhythm and arm pump but shortens the steps.
The upper body keeps the jog's forward hunch; a robed run should be more upright — a spine factor like the leg one would fix it.
The shoulder mantle lifts at the back when the arms swing back (it copies the shoulder weights). It wants weights on the spine only — a step-7 tidy.
A foot coming out UNDER the hem is allowed (that is what a robe looks like running); only crossing the cloth's wall counts as a poke-through.

title: Step 7 — swap-in runtime: one mesh and one texture per character, three distance versions, Chibi 2's API, ?renderer=chibi4 in Thousandvale
how: tools/blender/step7_export.py (~30 s per character) exports one GLB each (avatar-3d/chibi4/models/mage.glb 3.2 MB, elf.glb 3.5 MB): the 61-bone skeleton (MakeHuman's 53 + 8 skirt bones), 8 clips (idle, walk, run, cast, attack, hit, death, talk; the mage's walk and run with step 6's robe stride and a straighter spine — still 0 feet through the robe), body + eyes + brows + lashes + hair + outfit joined into ONE mesh, their pictures copied into ONE 2048 texture, and the same mesh at 40% and 15% of its triangles for distance. js/chibi4.js createChibi4Character(avatar) loads it and answers the same calls as Chibi 2 (setAnim, update, stats, metrics, dispose...); instances share the download. compare.html shows Chibi 2 and Chibi 4 side by side with the same clip and measures them. In Thousandvale, adding ?renderer=chibi4 to the URL gives the PLAYER a Chibi 4 body (7 lines in js/client/actors.js; everyone else stays Chibi 2; any error falls back to Chibi 2).

The near version is heavy (35k triangles) because MakeHuman's body is ~16k triangles before clothes and the elf's braid is 12k on its own. A lighter hair model and MakeHuman's own low-poly body would halve it.

Only 8 clips (Chibi 2 has ~90); no wave, guard, jump, weapon holds or mount seat.

title: Step 8 — Tripo3D (tripo3d.ai): an AI image-to-3D model from the Codex reference
how: The owner's friend built his game's humanoids with Tripo3D. Feed it the Codex reference, then rig and clean it in Blender. Needs a Tripo account/API key from the owner (the Blender MCP add-on's Tripo hook is Premium only).

title: Step 9 — the modular kit: one skeleton per body, every garment, hair and hat its own piece, assembled and recoloured at runtime
how: tools/blender/step9_kit.py (~2.5 min per body type) builds a kit per body type (male = the mage's sliders, female = the elf's) into models/kit/<body>/: body.glb (the 61-bone skeleton + body, eyes, brows and lashes, with pointed elf ears as a morph target), 13 garments (robe, mantle, sleeves, low boots, undershirt, jerkin, trousers, knee boots, bracers, pauldrons, tabard, scabbard, wizard hat) and 6 CC0 MakeHuman hair styles, each its own GLB skinned to the same bones; ONE colour atlas and ONE tint mask for all of them; 67 clips in two files (14 needed at once, the rest fetched after). Both outfits are measured off BOTH bodies, so any garment fits either body. Every vertex carries the list of garments that cover it (the hide mask): the runtime drops any triangle under something being worn — body under the robe, jerkin under the robe, hair under the hat — so mixing pieces never pokes through. js/chibi4-kit.js puts a character together from Chibi 2's avatar JSON (or avatar.chibi4 = { body, race, hair, garments }), copies the kept triangles of every piece into ONE geometry per distance (one draw call per character), shares downloads and merged outfits between characters, and recolours each garment's main and second colour plus the skin tone in the shader (a uniform write, no rebuild). Clips: Quaternius' CC0 library (35 copied, 4 mirrored for the left hand, jump = start+air+land, stand-up = a fall played backwards, sleep = a fall's last frame), 21 emotes authored on top of them (wave, point, salute, cheer, clap, bow, nod, head shake, shrug, laugh, folded arms, look around, stretch, pray, drink, guard, kick, spin, ride at a walk and a gallop, sit on the ground) and a robe-stride twin of walk, run, sprint and formal walk that the runtime plays whenever a floor-length robe is worn. All 96 Chibi 2 clip names map: 53 to the action itself, 43 to the nearest clip. Owner feedback folded in: everything is meshopt-compressed with gltfpack (step 7's mage.glb 3.17 MB -> 0.92 MB, the kit body 1.78 MB -> 0.34 MB, no visible change: positions and UVs stay full precision), and in Thousandvale ?renderer=chibi4 the download starts at page start, the player gets the Chibi 2 body at once and swaps to Chibi 4 when it is ready. The 'right leg bent backwards' was the trousers: copied their bone weights from a body with the legs hidden, so they took the hip's and foot's weights and never bent at the knee; garments now copy from the whole body (only the robe copies from the hidden one, so it follows the spine), checked per garment (trousers: 99.7% of vertices on the bone the body under them uses).

notes: Load numbers (tests/chibi4.spec.js, throttled to 10 Mbps with 40 ms latency, cache off): the mage player needs 10 files, 1.69 MB: download 1.75 s, decode 41 ms, assembled at 1.78 s, first frame +0.58 s (most of that is compiling shaders on this GPU-less VM). The elf: 13 files, 1.86 MB, 1.94 s + 0.54 s. Same files from the local server: ready in 0.29 s. Before: step 7's mage.glb alone was 3.17 MB uncompressed, and Thousandvale only started fetching it once the player body was built, behind the zone downloads.

In Thousandvale with ?renderer=chibi4 the player now gets the Chibi 2 body at once and swaps to the Chibi 4 kit body when it is ready (same spot, facing, clip and mount); the kit download starts at page start. Everyone else is still Chibi 2.

Clips are shared by every character of a body type (one file pair per body). They cannot be shared between the two bodies: the same retargeted clip differs by up to 15 degrees at the thighs and 80 at the toes, because each body's rest pose is its own.

The far versions matter most: 50 characters with full detail at every distance draw 1.53M triangles and a frame costs ~6x more. Evaluating far characters' animation every 2nd/3rd frame made no measurable difference here: on this VM the time goes into skinning vertices on the CPU, not into the animation mixer. Fewer bone influences per vertex for far versions was not tried (on a real GPU skinning is cheap; needs a real-PC measurement first).
A new outfit costs ~70 ms to assemble the first time (merging three distance versions); repeats are cached by outfit, so a crowd of the same uniform costs nothing extra.

Codex leftovers from steps 4–5, done this step: the elf's back view (ref/warrior-back.png, Codex) is now projected onto her clothes, and her braid is Codex-painted (textures/elf-hair.png; the raw Codex picture is textures/elf-hair-codex.png) instead of the no-AI colour-ramp stand-in.

Weak spots: inner layers (undershirt, trousers) were painted from the reference too, so where the tabard or jerkin covered them in the picture they carry a little of that paint when worn alone; the male body's beard is painted on the skin (every male face has it); only one hat model; no weapons in the hands yet (attach() puts any object on a hand bone); mounts still expect Chibi 2's seat.
